content.title: About
content.content: Aspartame is a low‑calorie artificial sweetener derived from the amino acids phenylalanine and aspartic acid. The powder form is convenient for precise dosing in cooking, baking, and beverages. It is about 200 times sweeter than sugar but contributes virtually no calories.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Aspartame was approved by the FDA in 1981 and has since become a common ingredient in diet sodas and low‑calorie foods.
Its sweetness comes from the combination of two amino acids rather than from sugar itself.
Aspartame degrades above 120 °C, so it is usually added to products after heat treatment.
In many countries (e.g., Japan) aspartame is labeled as E951.
It is safe for the general population but contraindicated for people with phenylketonuria (PKU).

items.title: Reduced calorie intake
items.content: Replacing sugar with aspartame helps lower the energy density of meals while preserving sweetness.

items.title: Supports blood glucose control
items.content: Aspartame does not raise blood sugar levels, making it suitable for individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Preserves taste profile
items.content: Unlike some sweeteners, aspartame leaves no bitter aftertaste and mimics sugar closely.

items.title: Phenylketonuria
items.content: People with PKU must avoid aspartame because they cannot metabolize phenylalanine.

items.title: Thermal instability
items.content: At high temperatures aspartame breaks down, forming methanol and other compounds, so it is not recommended for high‑heat baking.

items.title: Individual sensitivity
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience headaches or allergic‑type reactions, though scientific evidence is limited.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add aspartame powder to cold or warm drinks, yogurts, desserts, and sauces after cooking is finished. Typical dosage is indicated on the package – about 1 g of powder replaces roughly 200 g of sugar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a dry, cool place in a tightly sealed container to prevent moisture absorption. For long‑term storage, keep refrigerated, but protect from direct sunlight.
